title: An efficient algorithm for approximate shadow Hamiltonian simulation
authors: Abhijit Chakraborty, Bharath Sambasivam, Karunya Shirali, Hunter Nelson, Mafalda Ramôa, Sophia E. Economou, Edwin Barnes
abstract: We propose an efficient algorithm based on shadow Hamiltonian simulation to approximately simulate the real-time dynamics of observables under time-independent Hamiltonians. Shadow Hamiltonian simulation works at the level of the operator algebra generated by the observables through commutators with the Hamiltonian. Exactly encoding the quantum state in this picture is generally inefficient for interacting systems due to the exponential growth of the operator algebra. Our algorithm overcomes this bottleneck by systematically identifying the elements of the algebra most relevant to the target observables. This targeted approach is a controlled approximation that yields a highly efficient quantum state encoding that substantially reduces the size of the qubit register required to perform the time evolution using the shadow Hamiltonian. We propose two main pruning schemes, one based on a predefined operator basis and another on a constructed Krylov basis. We also present a hybrid scheme that builds a Krylov basis within a pruned algebra in the predefined basis. We benchmark our algorithm using lattice spin systems in one and two dimensions, for both one- and higher-point correlators as observables.
summary: The paper presents an advanced algorithm to simulate the time evolution of observables in complex quantum many-body systems by employing shadow Hamiltonian simulation. It introduces three pruning techniques—predefined basis, Krylov basis, and hybrid—to drastically reduce the size of the required operator algebra representation. This efficiency improvement makes simulating dynamics for interacting systems feasible on current or near-future quantum hardware.
main_problem: Developing an efficient algorithm for approximate shadow Hamiltonian simulation to track the real-time dynamics of observables under time-independent Hamiltonians.
main_result: The proposed hybrid pruning scheme significantly reduces the required qubit register size compared to pure Krylov or predefined basis methods, enabling simulations on larger systems.
method: It uses a targeted approximation by constructing a pruned operator algebra ($ ar{S}_O$) based on three schemes: predefined basis, adaptive Krylov basis, and a hybrid combination of both.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked using lattice spin systems in one and two dimensions, applicable to general many-body Hamiltonians like the MFIM or PLIM.
key_observables: Time evolution expectation values $\langle  ar{O}(t) angle$, higher-order correlation functions, and Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators (OTOCs).
important_parameters: Truncation thresholds ($\epsilon, \epsilon_1, \epsilon_2$), system size ($N$), and the ratio of field strengths to interaction couplings ($h_z$ vs $J$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that restricting the operator basis to elements relevant to the target observable yields a sufficiently accurate approximation, overcoming the exponential growth bottleneck.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the three pruning schemes (FIG. 1), compare shadow register size scaling across methods (TABLE I), and show accuracy vs. system size or field strength effects in MFIM simulations (Figs. S2-S4).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the mathematical framework of shadow simulation, proposes and analyzes three basis construction/pruning schemes (Predefined, Krylov, Hybrid), benchmarks these methods on lattice spin models, and discusses parameter regimes where pruning efficiency breaks down.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses resource scaling in simulating quantum dynamics for interacting systems, which is a major bottleneck in both theoretical condensed matter physics and practical quantum computing simulations.

Three schemes (predeﬁned basis, Krylov basis, and hybrid) can be used to build a shadow operator basis S containing important operators to ¯O under commutation with H. The shadow state encodes the expectation values of these observables on the physical state and can provide a more eﬃcient mapping onto ⌈log2 K⌉< N qubits. The shadow state is evolved by the shadow Hamiltonian HS, and measured in the computational basis to obtain the approximate real-time evolution of ¯O.
